entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen9908" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Talismanic Song in Time of War and Pestilence</title> <div sID="gen9909" type="x-p"/> The primeval song is followed by an anonymous song (inscribed by the lxx without any warrant τῷ Δαυίδ), the time of whose composition cannot be determined; and it is only placed in this order because the last verse accords with the last verse but one of Ps 90. There the revelation of Jahve’s work is prayed for, and here Jahve promises: <hi type="italic">I will grant him to see My salvation</hi>; the “work of Jahve” is His realized “salvation.” The two Psalms also have other points of contact, e.g., in the מעון referred to God (vid., <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi>, p. 60). <div eID="gen9909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9910" type="x-p"/> In this Psalm, the Invocavit Psalm of the church, which praises the protecting and rescuing grace which he who believingly takes refuge in God experiences in all times of danger and distress,<note placement="foot">Hence in J. <hi type="italic">Shabbath</hi> 8, col. 2, and <hi type="italic">Midrash</hi> <hi type="italic">Shocher</hi> <hi type="italic">tob</hi> on <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> and elsewhere, it is called, together with <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1-Ps.3.8">Psa 3:1-8</reference>, (פגעים) שיר פגועין, a song of occurrences, i.e., a protective (or talismanic) song in times of dangers that may befall one, just as Sebald Heyden’s Psalm-song, “He who is in the protection of the Most High and resigns himself to God,” is inscribed “Preservative against the pestilence.”</note> the relation of <reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference> to <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> meets us at the very beginning as a perplexing riddle. If we take <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> as a clause complete in itself, then it is tautological. If we take אמר in <reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference> as a participle (Jerome, <hi type="italic">dicens</hi>) instead of אמר, ending with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> because a construct from (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Psa 94:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.136.6">Psa 136:6</reference>), then the participial subject would have a participial predicate: “He who sitteth is saying,” which is inelegant and also improbable, since אמר in other instances is always the <hi type="italic">1st pers. fut</hi>. If we take אמר as <hi type="italic">1st pers. fut</hi>. and <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> as an apposition of the subject expressed in advance: as such an one who sitteth.... I say, then we stumble against יתלונן; this transition of the participle to the finite verb, especially without the copula (וּבצל), is confusing. If, however, we go on and read further into the Psalm, we find that the same difficulty as to the change of person recurs several times later on, just as in the opening. Olshausen, Hupfeld, and Hitzig get rid of this difficulty by all sorts of conjectures. But a reason for this abrupt change of the person is that dramatic arrangement recognised even in the Targum, although awkwardly indicated, which, however, as first of all clearly discerned by J. D. Michaelis and Maurer. There are, to wit, two voices that speak (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.121.1-Ps.121.8">Psa 121:1-8</reference>), and at last the voice of Jahve comes in as a third. His closing utterance, rich in promise, forms, perhaps not unaccidentally, a seven-line strophe. Whether the Psalm came also to be executed in liturgical use thus with several voices, perhaps by three choirs, we cannot tell; but the poet certainly laid it out dramatically, as the translation represents it. In spite of the many echoes of earlier models, it is one of the freshest and most beautiful Psalms, resembling the second part of Isaiah in its light-winged, richly coloured, and transparent diction.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1-Ps.91.2">Psa 91:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9911" type="x-p"/> As the concealing One, God is called עליון, the inaccessibly high One; and as the shadowing One שׁדּי, the invincibly almighty One. Faith, however, calls Him by His covenant name (<hi type="italic">Heilsname</hi>) יהוה and, with the suffix of appropriation, אלהי (<hi type="italic">my</hi> God). In connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference> we are reminded of the expressions of the Book of Job, <reference osisRef="Job.39.28">Job 39:28</reference>, concerning the eagle’s building its nest in its eyrie. According to the accentuation, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.91.2">Psa 91:2</reference></hi> ought to be rendered with Geier, “<hi type="italic">Dicit: in Domino meo (or Domini) latibulum</hi>, etc.” But the combination אמר לה is more natural, since the language of address follows in both halves of the verse.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.91.3-Ps.91.9">Psa 91:3-9</reference> יקושׁ, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.5">Pro 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.26">Jer 5:26</reference>, is the dullest toned from for יקושׁ or יוקשׁ, Psa 124:7. What is meant is death, or “he who has the power of death,” <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb 2:14</reference>, cf. 2Ti 2:26. “The snare of the fowler” is a figure for the peril of one’s life, Ecc 9:12. In connection with <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">Psa 91:4</reference> we have to call to mind <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference> : God protects His own as an eagle with its large strong wing. אברה is <hi type="italic">nom. unitatis</hi>, a pinion, to אבר, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Isa 40:31</reference>; and the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הסך, from סכך, with the dative of the object, like the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.140.8">Psa 140:8</reference>, signifies to afford covering, protection. The ἅπαξ λεγ. סחרה, according to its stem-word, is that which encompasses anything round about, and here beside צנּה, a weapon of defence surrounding the body on all sides; therefore not corresponding to the Syriac <hi type="italic">sḥārtā'</hi>, a stronghold (סהר, מסגּרת), but to Syriac <hi type="italic">sabrā'</hi>, a shield. The Targum translates צנּה with תּריסא, θυρεός, and סחרה with עגילא, which points to the round <hi type="italic">parma</hi>. אמתּו is the truth of the divine promises. This is an impregnable defence (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) in war-times, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.5">Psa 91:5</reference>, against nightly surprises, and in the battle by day; (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) in times of pestilence, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.6">Psa 91:6</reference>, when the destroying angel, who passes through and destroys the people (<reference osisRef="Exod.11.4">Exo 11:4</reference>), can do no harm to him who has taken refuge in God, either in the midnight or the noontide hours. The future יהלך is a more rhythmical and, in the signification to rage (as of disease) and to vanish away, a more usual form instead of ילך. The lxx, Aquila, and Symmachus erroneously associate the demon name שׁד with ישׁוּד. It is a metaplastic (as if formed from שׁוּד morf de) future for ישׁד, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.29.6">Pro 29:6</reference>, ירוּן, and <reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Isa 42:4</reference>, ירוּץ, <hi type="italic">frangetur</hi>. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.91.7">Psa 91:7</reference></hi> a hypothetical protasis: <hi type="italic">si cadant</hi>; the preterite would signify <hi type="italic">cediderint</hi>, Ew. §357, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. With רק that which will solely and exclusively take place is introduced. Burk correctly renders: <hi type="italic">nullam cum peste rem habebis, nisi ut videas</hi>. Only a spectator shalt thou be, and that with thine own eyes, being they self inaccessible and left to survive, conscious that thou thyself art a living one in contrast with those who are dying. And thou shalt behold, like Israel on the night of the Passover, the just retribution to which the evil-doers fall a prey. שׁלּמה, recompense, retribution, is a hapaxlegomenon, cf. שׁלּמים, Isa 34:8. Ascribing the glory to God, the second voice confirms or ratifies these promises.
